## Article Anion Etching for Accessing Rapid and Deep Self-Reconstruction of Precatalysts for Water Oxidation

Rapid and deep self-reconstruction (SELF-RECON) was achieved through rational design of the precatalyst. The obtained core-shell nanowired precatalyst (NiMoFeO@NC) consists of NiMoO4 nanoparticles (core) and NiFe/NiFeOx nanoparticles in N-doped carbons (shell). The SELF-RECON process was facilitated by rapid MoO4 2 dissolution in the core of NiMoFeO@NC and fast formation of NiOOH with Fe incorporation simultaneously, which was monitored and demonstrated by in situ Raman experiments. The obtained SELF-RECONCAT outperforms NiMoFeO@NC, with ultralow overpotentials and extraordinary longterm stability.

## Article Anion Etching for Accessing Rapid and Deep Self-Reconstruction of Precatalysts for Water Oxidation

Yang Wang,1,3,10 Yinlong Zhu,1,10 Shenlong Zhao,5,10 Sixuan She,9 Feifei Zhang,1 Yu Chen,6

Timothy Williams,6 Thomas Gengenbach,7 Lianhai Zu,1 Haiyan Mao,3 Wei Zhou,9 Zongping Shao,9

Huanting Wang,1 Jing Tang,2,* Dongyuan Zhao,1,4,11,* and Cordelia Selomulya1,8,*

SUMMARY Transition metal-based nanomaterials represent an emerging class of highly active and low-cost precatalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in alkaline electrolyzers. However, most OER precatalysts undergo slow or incomplete self-reconstructions to generate real active sites, which is a time-consuming process for achieving high OER performance. Thus, we report a new class of OER precatalysts that can achieve highly active OER species by a rapid and deep self-reconstruction (denoted by SELF-RECON). The precatalysts with a core-shell structure comprising NiMoO4 (core) and NiFe/Ni- FeOx nanoparticles in N-doped amorphous carbons (shell) (denoted by NiMoFeO@NC), can realize rapid MoO4 2 dissolution and fast formation of NiOOH with Fe incorporation simultaneously. In situ Raman spectroscopy together with electron microscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and electrochemical tests indicate that the obtained NiFeOOH/NiFe-LDH after SELF-RECON behave as the real active species that outperform NiMoFeO@NC, with ultralow overpotentials and extraordinary long-term stability.

## INTRODUCTION

Renewable energy technologies are expected not only to satisfy the growing energy demand but also to mitigate the increase of greenhouse gas emissions.1–3 Nevertheless, the intermittent nature of renewable energy sources, primarily solar and wind, has so far impeded their large-scale practical applications. To tackle this issue, electrocatalytic water splitting, which produces hydrogen from water at room/low temperature without using additional reactants, has emerged as a promising solution for renewables intermittency, particularly with the possibility of driving the process using electrical energy generated from renewable sources.4–6 Generally, water splitting involves two-electron and four-electron transfer reactions, occurring at the cathode and the anode, respectively. In addition, it is well established that the anodical oxygen evolution reaction (OER) is the main bottleneck in electrochemical water splitting, owing to its large overpotential and slow reaction kinetics involving multiple electron and proton transfers.7–10

Thus, improving the catalytic activity and accelerating the kinetics on the anodic side are highly desirable in order to achieve high-performance electrolyzers.

To date, various noble metal and non-noble metal-based materials (e.g., transition metals and their derivatives) have been fabricated as efﬁcient catalysts for electrocatalytic oxygen evolution.11–20 Several studies regarding the activity origin of OER

Progress and Potential

A key challenge in rationally designing efﬁcient electrolyzers is to achieve high-performance oxygen evolution reaction (OER) electrocatalysts. In situ generated (oxy)hydroxides during OER are usually regarded as real active sites for precatalysts, but most OER precatalysts have slow selfreconstructions. Thus, the rational design of precatalysts that can rapidly generate active OER species is highly desirable. We have fabricated a new OER precatalyst that undergoes rapid self-reconstruction by fast anion etching and bimetallic activation (denoted by SELF-RECON). In situ Raman spectra, electron microscopy, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicate that the obtained NiFe- (oxy)hydroxides after SELF- RECON behave as the active OER species with extraordinary OER performance and robust stability. Our work demonstrates that anion-etching-induced SELF- RECON is a promising design strategy for fabrication of highly active catalysts for electrolyzers and other energy conversion devices.

have suggested that the in situ generation of oxy-hydroxides (MOOH) after selfreconstruction under OER conditions is crucial for their high catalytic activities observed in OER catalysts.21–24 Nevertheless, because of the relatively large size and/or the poor structural ﬂexibility of many precatalysts, most self-reconstructions triggered by electro-oxidation during the OER process generally occur exclusively on the precatalysts’ surface. This results in the formation of the typical core-shell (oxide@oxyhydroxides) structures,25–27 wherein the active sites are buried in the inner components of the core and therefore cannot exhibit OER activity.

Much recent work shows that downsizing the precatalysts and increasing their crystal ﬂexibility are promising strategies for facilitating structural reconstruction and thereby achieving favorable OER activity.28 However, it is difﬁcult to avoid the aggregation of nanoparticles with the real active sites during the conventional synthesis processes, which include chemical oxidation or thermal treatment. Although Liu et al. reported that lithiation can be employed to reduce the size of nickel particles to facilitate self-reconstruction, this method is limited by its sophisticated fabrication process.28 Therefore, another more efﬁcient process such as electrochemical etching is highly desirable to facilitate the self-reconstruction. For example, etching of Cl in Co2(OH)3Cl29 enables Co2(OH)3Cl to be reconstructed into OER active CoOOH, which results in substantially enhanced OER performance. Furthermore, etching of F in NiFe-OH-F, even only to the extent of surface self-reconstruction, is also reported to improve its OER performance.30 However, in both NiFe-OH-F and Co2(OH)3Cl, the self-reconstruction process is relatively slow with hundreds of CV cycles required to achieve the maximum OER activity. For the self-reconstruction in NiSe@NiOOH, such processes can even take up to 8 h for completion.31 Therefore, a rapid and deep self-reconstruction by rational design of precatalysts would be highly desirable, especially if accompanied by synergistic bimetallic activation for each active site.

Here, we have fabricated a core-shell nanowired precatalyst using a facile Prussian blue analog (PBA)-based ion-exchange method followed by low-temperature annealing. The obtained precatalyst features a uniform core-shell structure, composed of NiFe/NiFeOx nanoparticles anchored on NiMoO4 in amorphous carbon (NiMo- FeO@NC). This favorable structure can facilitate the rapid and deep self-reconstruction process by rapid etching of MoO4 2 from NiMoO4 cores and simultaneous incorporation of Fe in the Ni-(oxy)hydroxide shells. The obtained SELF-RECONCAT exhibits a remarkable OER catalytic performance, requiring overpotentials of only 270 and 290 mV to obtain 50 and 100 mA cm2, respectively, with negligible degradation after 24 h of OER electrolysis at 100 mA cm2.

## RESULTS

Synthesis and Characterization of NiMoFeO@NC The core-shell structured NiMoFeO@NC was synthesized by using a PBA-based ionexchange method which reported in a previous work.32 In brief, NiMoO4 was grown on nickel foam (NiMoO4), followed by immersion in K3[Fe(CN)6] solution at 90C for 10 min to obtain NiMoO4@PBA (KNi[Fe(CN)6], hereafter is denoted as PBA), which was then calcined at 300C for 2 h in N2 atmosphere to produce NiMoFeO@NC (Figure 1). X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Figure 2G) show that, compared with that of NiMoO4, the new diffraction peaks observed in NiMoO4@PBA can be assigned to KNi[Fe(CN)6] (PDF no. 01-089-8978), indicating the successful synthesis of PBA on NiMoO4. After the calcination, all the diffraction peaks from NiMoFeO@NC (Figure 2G) can be assigned to NiMoO4 (PDF no. 01-079-7552), indicative of the

From scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images (Figures 2A–2C), it can be observed that the surface of a representative NiMoO4 nanowire is smooth with an average diameter of ~200 nm. High-magniﬁcation transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images reveal a typical lattice fringes with a d-spacing of 0.65 nm, which matches well with the (010) planes of NiMoO4 (Figures S2A and S2B). Notably, numerous defects can be observed in the NiMoO4 wires (yellow circles in Figure S2B), which enables NiMoO4 to be readily converted into PBA, despite the highly crystalline and preferentially oriented nature of NiMoO4 indicated by selected area electron diffraction (SAED) patterns (Figure S2C). After ion exchange for 10 min, PBA crystals can be grown on the surface of NiMoO4 wire (Figure 2B). In a typical Ni- MoO4@PBA nanowire (Figure S2D), the diameter of the NiMoO4 core is ca. 100 nm while the PBA shell is 40–60 nm. After a subsequent calcination, the Ni- MoO4@PBA wires can be transformed into NiMoO4 and NiFe/NiFeOx nanoparticles in N-doped carbon (denoted by NiMoFeO@NC) with a rough surface (Figure 2C). Several thin NiMoFeO@NC nanowires feature hollow structures due to the Kirkendall effect during the ion-exchange process (the red circle in Figure 2C). The inner diameter of the tubes is measured to be ca. 46 nm with wall thickness of ca. 60 nm (Figure 2D). The walls of the NiMoFeO@NC nanotubes are composed of tiny nanoparticles within 10 nm (Figures S3A and S3B). Voids or defects are distributed on the boundaries between the nanoparticles after calcination (Figures S3B and S3D). The SAED patterns of NiMoFeO@NC show the polycrystalline nature of NiMoO4, NiFe, and NiFeOx (Figure 2F). Rapid and Deep Self-Reconstruction and OER Performance of SELF- RECONCAT The OER activity of NiMoFeO@NC in 1.0 M KOH was evaluated using polarization curves obtained from linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) with a scan rate of 5 mV s1. All the potential values presented in this work were iR-corrected and referenced to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) unless indicated otherwise. After just ten LSV scans (Figure 3A), the performance of NiMoFeO@NC is shown to be significantly improved due to the SELF-RECON process (denoted by SELF-RECONCAT).

Compared with those of NiMoFeO@NC, NiMoO4-SR, and NiMoO4, the Tafel slope of SELF-RECONCAT has the lowest value of 66.6 mV dec1, indicating its superior kinetics (Figure 3D). The charge-transfer resistance obtained from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is another factor that can be used to describe the kinetics of an electrochemical process on the catalysts. The diameter of the semi-circle in the Nyquist plot represents the value of charge-transfer resistance, with a smaller diameter indicating a lower charge-transfer resistance during the electrochemical process. SELF- RECONCAT has the smallest charge-transfer resistance of 0.37 U (Figure 3E), while those of NiMoO4-SR and NF are as high as 2.2 and 6.1 U, respectively. Note that no EIS data are provided for either NiMoO4 or NiMoFeO@NC as both are unstable under EIS conditions. After being subjected to a current density of 100 mA cm2 for 24 h, the overpotential of SELF-RECONCAT shows a negligible increase, indicative of its robust stability. The overpotential shifts slightly toward the positive end in LSV plots after 24 h of electrolysis at 100 mA cm2, possibly because a part of the catalyst is detached from the Ni foam owing to the violent release of O2 gas (Figure S6A). In contrast, when the electrolysis current for the chronopotentiometry test is reduced to 50 mA cm2, after 24 h of electrolysis the LSV plot completely coincides with that of SELF-RECONCAT prior to 24 h of electrolysis (Figure S6B). This indicates that the SELF-RECONCAT is highly stable and able to retain its excellent OER performance at high current densities during long-term chronopotentiometry testing. In addition, after 24 h of OER electrolysis the SELF-RECONCAT still maintains the nanowire structure with the same subunits and elements, which further demonstrates its robust stability (Figures S8–S10). Such extraordinary OER performance of SELF-RECONCAT enables it to rival other well-known high-performance catalysts (Table S1) and to rank among the most active alkaline OER catalysts.

In Situ Raman Spectroelectrochemistry for Self-Reconstruction To investigate the dynamic self-reconstruction under OER reaction conditions, we employed in situ Raman spectroelectrochemistry with controlled potentials in 1 M KOH electrolyte. We ﬁrstly investigated the local surface crystal structure of freshly prepared NiMoFeO@NC samples under open circuit potential conditions (i.e., no extra potentials applied). All the detectable bands can be assigned to Mo-O vibrations with 350, 815–900, and 939 cm1 ascribed to y4, y3, and y1(2Ag) vibration modes of Mo-O in NiMoO4, respectively (Figure 4A).35,36 When bias voltages were applied and gradually increased on NiMoFeO@NC, the intensity of Mo-O bands was accordingly reduced and completely undetectable at 1.65 V (versus RHE) due to the dissolution of MoO4 2 during the SELF-RECON process under OER conditions. Meanwhile, more signiﬁcant surface structure conversion was noticed when the potential was increased to 1.4 V (versus RHE). The appearance of two well-deﬁned Raman bands located at 474 and 557 cm1, ascribed to the Eg (Ni-O) bending vibration mode and A1g (Ni-O) stretching vibration mode, respectively, indicates the formation of g-NiOOH.37 Similar potential-dependent structural changes also took place in NiMoO4 (Figure S11). Two extra broad bands located at 558 and 684 cm1 appearing in NiMoFeO@NC compared with NiMoO4 are likely assigned to Ni-O and Fe-O vibrations in NiFeOx, respectively (Figure S12).38 Fe from NiMoFeO@NC can further incorporate into NiOOH for structural modiﬁcation during the self-reconstruction process. The intensity ratio between the bands at 557 and 474 cm1 (I557/I474) can work as an indicator of OER activity in Ni-Fe systems, with the higher ratio corresponding to the superior OER performance. When the potential applied was increased to 1.65 V (versus RHE), only the two bands at 557 and 474 cm1 retained and the intensity ratio I557/I474 was higher in NiMoFeO@NC than

XPS Spectra of NiMoFeO@NC and SELF-RECONCAT X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was applied to further study the activation process. It should be noted that although XPS can be a very useful technique for studying catalysts, it has several limitations when applied to complex hybrid materials as in the present case. In NiMoO4, the peak shape of the XPS spectrum of Ni 2p (Figure S16) suggests that Ni is most likely to be present as a hydroxide forming on the surface of Ni- MoO4 with 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 peaks at 856.2 and 873.8 eV, respectively, along with broad satellites at higher binding energies. In comparison with NiMoO4 with Ni species in the Ni2+ state, in NiMoFeO@NC (Figure 5A) the Ni 2p1/2 and Ni 2p3/2 spectra are deconvoluted into four peaks, located at ~855.0, 872.4, ~856.6, and 874.0 eV, indicating the presence of Ni(III) species, which is likely due to the formation of nickel-iron oxides on the surface of NiMoFeO@NC.41 An overall broader Ni 2p3/2 peak shape is also observed in SELF-RECONCAT (Figure 5C) where, due to the OER process in alkaline solutions, metal hydroxides might have formed on the surface of the samples. The relative increase of the high-binding-energy peak within the convolution and the overall broadening of the total peak suggest a slight increase of Ni3+ with respect to Ni2+ in SELF-RECONCAT than the precatalyst (NiMoFeO@NC) after the SELF-RECON process.

The O 1s spectra are always complex, arising from multiple sources. Generally, contributions at or below ca. 529.5 eV can be assigned to lattice oxygen in metal oxides, whereas peaks at higher binding energies (531–534 eV) may be due to hydroxides, oxygen defects, organic oxygen, and possibly adsorbed water. The main peak in pure NiMoO4 is most likely a superposition of oxide and hydroxide contributions (Figure S17). In the case of NiMoFeO@NC, the metal oxide contribution becomes more dominant (Figure 5B), whereas after SELF-RECON the relative intensity of the oxide peak in SELF-REC- ONCAT is markedly reduced and the component at 531–532 eV becomes more dominant due to the formation of NiFeOOH/NiFe-LDH (Figure 5D).

With the exception of NiMoO4, which does not contain Fe, the Fe 2p core-level spectrum of all samples (Figure 5E) displays a broad peak shape, with the 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 peaks being measured at 711.4 and 724.5 eV, respectively. This broad peak probably represents a mixture of Fe oxides/hydroxides in NiMoFeO@NC and SELF-REC- ONCAT, most likely dominated by Fe3+.42 The Mo 3d spectra for both NiMoO4 (Figure S18) and NiMoFeO@NC (Figure 5F) exhibit two peaks at approximately 232.5 and 235.6 eV, respectively, indicating that Mo is in the Mo6+ state. However, in SELF-RECONCAT, Mo almost disappears due to the complete dissolution of MoO4 2 after the rapid and deep self-reconstruction.

## DISCUSSION

The precatalysts are designed to possess both componential and structural advantages to make them ideal for the SELF-RECON process. With respect to componential advantages, the precatalysts are supposed to not only have an etchable component to facilitate rapid and deep self-reconstruction, but also contain appropriate content of Fe for the activation of nickel oxides during self-reconstruction. Besides, carbon is also required in the catalysts to facilitate the fast electron transfer during

With regard to the structural advantages, core-shell nanowires comprising nanosized subunits with plenty of boundaries and voids are highly advisable to ensure the fast electrolyte transfer into the core of precatalysts for SELF-RECON. Bearing these factors in mind, a facile synthesis route composed of an ion-exchange process and low-temperature annealing is highly desirable to transform NiMoO4 (alkaline etchable) into target precatalysts. During the ion-exchange process, the periphery of NiMoO4 can be converted into a PBA shell (NiMoO4@PBA) due to a stronger coordination of Ni2+ toward [Fe(CN)6]3- than MoO4 2, following the Kirkendall effect, with a lower solubility of PBA (Ksp(Co-PBA) = 1.8 3 1015) compared with NiMoO4 (Ksp = 3.2 3 1012). The suitable content of Fe can be obtained by controlling the ion-exchange duration whereby prolonging the duration can result in more PBA, thus presenting more Fe in the precatalysts.

The transformation process of precatalysts from NiMoO4@PBA to NiMoFeO@NC was also studied. The calcination process was undertaken at 300C for 2 h under N2 ﬂow, during which both the NiMoO4 core and PBA shell underwent transformations. Although the original NiMoO4 precursor (chemical formula NiMoO4$0.7H2O) has a highly crystalline and preferentially oriented structure, it is susceptible to transformation into NiMoO4 nanoparticles by releasing the structural H2O molecules during calcination. This structural transformation is conﬁrmed by corresponding TEM images and SAED patterns. Additionally, the co-existing NiFe alloys and NiFeOx are derived from PBA shells in NiMoO4@PBA where PBA is converted into NiFe alloys and amorphous carbons, followed by partial transformation into NiFeOx when exposed to air. This is consistent with the previous reports showing that PBA tends to decompose into corresponding metal alloys with the residual CN transforming into amorphous carbon.44,45 The obtained amorphous carbon can prevent the aggregation of the active particles under heat treatment and retain the structure during anion etching.46,47 In addition, the carbon can also facilitate the electron transfer from the catalyst surface to the substrate to enable oxidation to take place on the catalyst surface, similar to the function of pyrochlore oxide in Co/Y2Ru2xCoxO7.48

Moreover, the annealing temperature is crucial to the fabrication of precatalysts. For example, when different annealing temperatures were used to treat Ni- MoO4@PBA, the obtained catalysts showed different catalytic performance (Figure S21), which could be ascribed to the formation of different subunits with various structures in the corresponding precatalysts. In our case, since we directly performed XRD characterization on the catalysts grown on nickel foams, the characteristic peaks of NiFe at (111) and (200) planes, similar to that of the bare nickel, can inevitably coincide with those from the nickel foam itself. Fortunately, the existence of NiFe alloys in NiMoFeO@NC can be conﬁrmed by the typical lattice fringes through the SAED patterns and TEM images. However, as the surface of these metal alloy nanoparticles is highly susceptible to oxidation to form oxides or hydroxides, no obvious signal of Ni0 or Fe0 was detected and shown in XPS spectra.49

During the SELF-RECON process of NiMoFeO@NC, MoO4 2 is drastically etched from the core (composed of NiMoO4 nanoparticles), accompanied by the incorporation of Fe into NiOOH on the shell to form highly active NiFeOOH/NiFe-LDH. This SELF-RECON process is conﬁrmed by in situ Raman results (Figures 4A and 4B). The abundant voids and defects in NiMoFeO@NC allow the electrolytes to easily transfer into the NiMoO4 cores. In addition, the small size of NiMoO4 nanoparticles in the core region enables them to fully interact with KOH electrolytes, thus favoring the rapid dissolution of MoO4 2 with an ECSA. The 6-fold increase of ECSA in SELF-RECONCAT compared with NiMoFeO@NC after the SELF-RECON is due to the enhanced conductivity and more exposure of accessible sites for redox reactions in SELF-RECONCAT, which is

According to in situ Raman spectra (Figure 4B), the higher ratio of I554/I476 (I denotes the intensity of the corresponding band) in SELF-RECONCAT compared with that of NiMoFeO@NC indicates the higher structural disorder caused by the incorporation of Fe into NiOOH. During SELF-RECON, the Fe incorporation is considered to occur through a dynamic dissolution-redeposition of Fe at the NiOOH/ electrolyte interface as evidenced by the work reported previously (Figure 4C).50–52 According to Table S2, after the fast etching process during SELF-RECON, the content of Fe and Ni decreases by 1%–3% due to the dissolution triggered by the drastic leaching of MoO4 2.50 The ﬁnal obtained SELF-RECONCAT shows as NiFeOOH/NiFe-LDH@NC (Fe:Ni = 0.26, Table S2) with the molar ratio of Fe/Ni within the optimized range (0.1– 0.55) to enhance OER activity of Ni oxides by Fe doping.30,53,54 It is widely accepted that Fe incorporation can completely alter the nature of the active sites by tuning the electronic structure of Ni oxides.55 Additionally, The OER activity of NiMoO4@PBA is essentially the same as that of NiMoO4 (Figure S22), which highlights the inertness of PBA. This is because PBA would spontaneously decompose in 1 M KOH solution, with Fe presenting as an anion of [Fe(CN)6]3, and thus could not be redeposited on NiOOH for incorporation. Hence, the active sites of NiMoO4@PBA should merely originate from NiMoO4. Conclusively, the source of Fe is crucial for the activation of nickel oxides.

Conclusion An efﬁcient way has been developed to prepare highly active OER catalysts through a rapid and deep self-reconstruction process that consists of fast anion etching and synergistic Fe incorporation. This rapid and deep self-reconstruction is demonstrated by in situ Raman spectra and triggered by the fast anion dissolution beneﬁting from the small size of subunits and core-shell structure of the precatalyst (NiMoFeO@NC). After SELF-RECON, the obtained SELF-RECONCAT exhibits an extraordinary OER performance, requiring overpotentials of only 270 and 290 mV to achieve 50 and 100 mA cm2, respectively, with negligible degradation after 24 h of OER electrolysis at 100 mA cm2. Such remarkable OER performance is attributed to the in situ generated active NiFeOOH/NiFe-LDH, ECSA, and fast electron transfer through carbon in the catalyst. Therefore, our ﬁndings open up a new avenue for the design and fabrication of high-performance OER catalysts for water electrolyzers and also inspire further studies in other electrocatalysts (e.g., CO2, N2 electrochemical reduction) with enhanced performance by SELF-RECON.
